newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Economic meeting loses vision of peaceful Mideast.
newsitem.headline: Economic meeting loses vision of peaceful Mideast.

text.p: This week's Middle East economic conference in Cairo is more likely to showcase the unresolved Arab-Israeli conflict than the vision of a peaceful, prosperous Middle East that drove past years' meetings.

The election of Israeli leader Benjamin Netanyahu last May on a platform that has paralysed hopes for peace with Syria and plunged negotiations with Palestinians into crisis has battered the prospects for economic cooperation.

"Everybody knows that without peace there is no hope for economic development," said Mitsuo Sakaba, deputy chief of mission at the Cairo embassy of Japan, which has been helping to underwrite the Middle East peace process.

The level of attendance and the actions of those at the Middle East and North Africa economic conference opening on Tuesday will probably reflect the changed politics. Last year's eagerness to hop aboard a deal-making bandwagon has faded.

Even some Israeli ministers, in contrast to those anxious to be seen at the inaugural gathering in Casablanca in 1994 and last year's conference in Amman, threatened to boycott the Cairo session over criticism of Israeli policies.

For months after the election of Netanyahu, Egypt pondered simply cancelling the conference, which Washington considers a showpiece of the new Middle East that its five years of peacemaking was designed to produce.
When Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak finally decided to proceed, he made clear his purpose was national interest, not advancing an increasingly elusive search for Middle East peace.
"This conference is not being held for Israel," he said. "We have asked all the world's major companies to attend and see development in Egypt."

Mubarak was underlining the reality that the Middle East and North Africa region needs investment. The World Bank calculated that the non-oil exports of the Arab countries, whose economies sank in recent years to the lowest growth rates in the world, are less than the exports of Finland.

Some countries, such as rapidly liberalising Egypt, may still attract foreign investment. Leaders, both Israeli and Arab, had moved in recent years to trim bureaucracy, eliminate investor-hostile regulations and privatise state-owned industries.
But all, Israel included, would be more attractive to investors if the threat of war that has hung over the region for decades was finally removed.

That virtuous circle -- political stability encouraging investment and further strengthening stability -- was an integral part of Washington's drive to end a half-century of Israel's isolation in the region.

Although progress was often difficult, many on both sides had considered the peace process irreversible. Arab and Israeli businessmen, who never before would have met in public, attended the Amman economic conference because they did not want to be left out of potentially profitable deals.
That certainty of peace is gone. Instead, old barriers have reappeared since Netanyahu defeated Prime Minister Shimon Peres, the chief Israeli driving force in peace talks, in the election in May.
Headlines in Israel now talk more of the danger of another war with Syria than the vision Peres expounded of Israel fully integrated into a peaceful and prosperous Middle East.

Netanyahu's uncompromising positions -- rejecting the "land-for-peace" basis of peace talks -- have drawn Arab threats to freeze normalising of ties. Complains have come even from Jordan, Israel's closest Arab friend and a country that rushed to make peace in 1994 in expectation of economic gains.

Palestinian businessmen, angry at the stalemate in their government's peace talks with Netanyahu and Israeli restrictions that are strangling their economy, decided this month not to send official representatives to the Cairo conference.

Israel said it would send five cabinet ministers. But Infrastructure Minister Ariel Sharon and, briefly, Agriculture Minister Rafael Eitan -- the men who directed the 1982 invasion of Lebanon and were held partly responsible for the massacre of hundreds of Palestinian refugees in Beirut -- blocked their departments' involvement over Egyptian criticism of Netanyahu.

The U.S. delegation will be headed by Secretary of State Warren Christopher. The man who had talked optimistically of a new era at the previous two conferences is leaving office in January with his dream of comprehensive peace unfulfilled and existing accomplishments in danger of falling apart.
